claims.claim: Sikhism is a monotheistic religion founded in the Punjab region of South Asia in the late 15th century by Guru Nanak (1469-1539).

Sikh tradition counts a line of ten human Gurus from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh (1666-1708); on Gobind Singh's death the Guruship passed to the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs have treated as the final, permanent Guru ever since.

The Guru Granth Sahib (Adi Granth) is a collection of hymns compiled by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, in 1604, holding about six thousand hymns by the Sikh Gurus and by other saints; Sikhs revere the book as a living Guru and show it the respect due to a human Guru.

Core Sikh teachings include belief in one God without form or gender; the equality of all people before God, expressed in rejection of caste-based distinctions and in women and men sharing equally in worship; seva (selfless service); and nam simran (remembering and meditating on God).
Sikh tradition records that Guru Nanak refused the sacred thread that marked caste status, insisting that people should be distinguished by their deeds and qualities rather than by birth.

In 1699 Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa, a community of initiated Sikhs, introducing the rite of initiation and the Five Ks: kesh (uncut hair), kara (steel bracelet), kanga (wooden comb), kaccha (cotton undergarment), and kirpan (steel sword).

The gurdwara is the Sikh place of congregational worship; the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib is what makes a building a gurdwara; gurdwaras contain no idols or statues; anyone of any faith may visit and is welcome.
Every gurdwara has a langar, a free kitchen where simple food is served to all visitors without charge, whatever their caste or faith; the term also names the communal meal itself.
Kirtan, the singing of hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib, is an essential part of Sikh worship; congregational worship may be led by any competent Sikh, male or female.
The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) at Amritsar is Sikhism's pre-eminent spiritual site, a gurdwara complex that includes a langar.

Sikhism today is a global tradition with tens of millions of followers, most of them in the Indian Punjab: BBC Religions reported 20 million Sikhs worldwide (2009) and 336,000 in the United Kingdom at the 2001 census with about 200 gurdwaras in Britain; Wikipedia's summary gives 25-30 million adherents; the Pluralism Project documents an active Sikh community in the United States.

Scholars and Sikhs describe Sikhism as a distinct tradition, not a synthesis of Hinduism and Islam: BBC Religions states that Guru Nanak's ideas drew on Hindu and Islamic thought but were 'far more than just a synthesis' and that he taught a faith 'quite distinct' from both, while Britannica notes that many Western scholars argue that in its earliest stage Sikhism was a movement within the Hindu tradition - an origins debate the lesson attributes rather than resolves.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Was earliest Sikhism a movement within the Hindu tradition?
positions: Britannica: 'many Western scholars argue that in its earliest stage Sikhism was a movement within the Hindu tradition'
BBC Religions: Guru Nanak began teaching a faith 'quite distinct from Hinduism and Islam'; his ideas were 'far more than just a synthesis'
Sikhs' own description of the tradition as founded by a divinely inspired Guru with its own scripture and community
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents Sikhism's distinct, independent character as the standard scholarly and Sikh description and attributes the origins debate explicitly rather than calling Sikhism a synthesis or adjudicating the question.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Who counts as a member of the Khalsa?
positions: BBC Religions (Guru Gobind Singh page): 'Today the Khalsa comprises all practising Sikhs'
BBC Religions (at a glance; Amrit ceremony page): the Khalsa is the community of men and women initiated into the Sikh faith; initiated Sikhs (Amritdhari) wear the Five Ks
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the Khalsa as the community of initiated Sikhs and notes that initiation through the Amrit ceremony is a distinct step, following the more precise at-a-glance and Amrit-ceremony descriptions.
